html:
The Soviet Union sent its army into Afghanistan in December 1979 to prop up a communist government facing revolt, and fought there for nearly ten years. Soviet troops killed the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin and installed Babrak Karmal in his place.

Against them stood the mujahideen, Islamic guerrilla bands armed and paid through Pakistan by the United States, Saudi Arabia and others, in one of the last big proxy fights of the Cold War. The Soviets held the cities and main roads; the guerrillas held the mountains and villages.

Perhaps a million or more Afghans died and about five million fled, most to camps in Pakistan and to Iran. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers were killed. Mikhail Gorbachev pulled the last troops out in February 1989.

The war drained Soviet money and morale shortly before the Soviet Union broke up. In Afghanistan it was followed by civil war and then the rise of the Taliban.
